title: The phases of the Moon
subtitle: Why the Moon changes shape, and when each phase is in the sky

sections.heading: Half lit, always
body: After this lesson you will be able to look at the Moon, name its phase, say roughly what time it rose and will set, and judge whether tonight is a good night for faint objects.

The Moon is a ball lit by the Sun, so half of it is always in sunlight. The phases are how much of that sunlit half is turned toward us as the Moon circles Earth. They have nothing to do with Earth's shadow, which touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

When the Moon is in the same direction as the Sun we face its dark side: new Moon. As it moves away from the Sun we see a thin sliver of the lit half, a crescent, which grows night by night. A quarter of the way round it looks half lit; this is called first quarter. Then it is gibbous, more than half lit, and when it is opposite the Sun we see the whole sunlit face: full Moon. The second half of the cycle runs the same shapes in reverse: gibbous, last quarter, crescent, new. One cycle takes 29.5 days. A growing Moon is called waxing and a shrinking one waning.

The lit edge always points to the Sun. From the northern hemisphere, an evening Moon lit on the right is waxing and a morning Moon lit on the left is waning. From the southern hemisphere the view is mirrored: the waxing evening Moon is lit on the left, the waning morning Moon on the right.

steps.caption: April 9, 2027, 8:30 pm, an hour after sunset, looking west from mid-northern latitudes. The Moon is three days past new: a thin crescent, 11% lit, two and a half fists up and following the Sun down.
Four evenings later at the same time: first quarter. The Moon is half lit and 66° high in the south-southwest, a quarter of the sky away from the Sun.

First quarter from mid-southern latitudes (34°S), on April 14 at 7 pm. Facing north, the half-lit Moon is a third of the way up the sky and lit on its left side: the side toward the Sun, which has set in the west, on your left.

highlights.label: First quarter, seen from the south

steps.caption: April 16: waxing gibbous, 82% lit, and now in the southeast at the same hour. Each night the Moon has been about 13° farther east.
April 20: full Moon, only just risen in the east-southeast. It came up at 7:50 pm, ten minutes after the Sun went down on the opposite side of the sky.
April 23, same time, facing east: no Moon. It will not rise until after 11 pm. The evening sky is dark again, and the waning Moon belongs to the late night and morning.

figures.caption: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun; its phase is how much of that lit half faces us. Slide through the month: at new Moon the lit half faces away, at first quarter we see half of it side-on, at full Moon all of it. The inset shows the Moon the way it looks from your hemisphere, with rough rising and setting times.

misconception.myth: The phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling across the Moon.
misconception.fact: Earth's shadow points away from the Sun and touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, at full Moon. A crescent Moon is close to the Sun in the sky, nowhere near Earth's shadow; we are simply seeing a thin edge of its sunlit half.

thinkAbout.question: If you stood on the near side of the Moon at new Moon, what would Earth look like?
thinkAbout.answer: A full Earth. At new Moon the Sun is behind the Moon and shining on the side of Earth that faces it. Earth's phases seen from the Moon are always the opposite of the Moon's phases seen from Earth. That full Earth is what lights the dark part of a thin crescent Moon with a faint grey glow: earthshine.

sections.heading: When each phase is up
body: Because the phase is set by the Moon's angle from the Sun, each phase keeps its own hours. A new Moon rises and sets with the Sun. A waxing crescent is in the west after sunset and sets in the evening. A first-quarter Moon is highest around sunset and sets around midnight. A full Moon rises at sunset and is up all night. A last-quarter Moon rises around midnight and is high at dawn. A waning crescent rises shortly before the Sun.

The Moon circles the sky, eastward along the zodiac, once in about 27 days: 13° per day, or its own width every hour. So each day Earth has to turn a little farther to bring it back into view, and moonrise comes later by about 50 minutes a day on average. The delay varies a lot with the season, from under half an hour to well over an hour.

steps.caption: The Moon at 8:30 pm on seven evenings, April 9 to 15, 2027, on a star chart. It steps east (left) about 13° a day, from Taurus through Gemini and Cancer into Leo, staying within 5° of the ecliptic line.

figures.caption: One real month, April to May 2027, worked out for your location: each column is a day from noon to the next noon, and the bar shows when the Moon is up. Crescents set in the evening, the full Moon is up all night, and waning phases move into the morning. Step through the days and compare each moonrise with the day before.

check.prompt: You want to see a waning crescent Moon. When and where should you look?
choices: Low in the east shortly before sunrise
Low in the west shortly after sunset
High in the sky at midnight
Low in the east at sunset
check.explanation: A waning crescent is a little west of the Sun, so it rises shortly before the Sun and is seen in the east at dawn.

sections.heading: The Moon and your observing
body: Moonlight is the countryside's light pollution. Around full Moon the sky is bright enough to wash out the Milky Way and the fainter stars even from a dark site, and faint constellations become hard to trace. In the city the bright stars and planets are unaffected. Deep-sky objects such as nebulae and galaxies are best hunted in the two weeks centered on new Moon, or at any time when the Moon is below the horizon.

For looking at the Moon itself, full Moon is the worst time. Sunlight then falls straight down on the surface, there are no shadows and it looks flat. The best views are along the terminator, the line between lunar day and night, where the Sun is rising or setting on the Moon and every crater and mountain casts a long shadow. Binoculars show it well any evening between crescent and gibbous.

figures.caption: The side of the Moon we never see from Earth, photographed from lunar orbit with the Sun shining on it. It gets as much sunlight as the near side: at new Moon it is in full daylight.

misconception.myth: The far side of the Moon is the 'dark side', always in darkness.
misconception.fact: The Moon keeps the same face toward Earth, so we never see the far side, but it gets just as much sunlight as the near side. At new Moon, when the side facing us is dark, the far side is fully lit. 'Far side' is the accurate name.

sections.tryIt: Find the Moon tonight and note its phase and the time. Tomorrow at the same time, see how far east it has moved (a little more than a fist) and how the lit part has changed. If you cannot find it in the evening, look around sunrise.

keyPoints: Phases come from our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth, not from Earth's shadow.
The cycle from new Moon to new Moon takes 29.5 days.
First quarter: high at sunset, sets around midnight. Full: rises at sunset, up all night. Last quarter: rises around midnight.
The Moon moves about 13° east per day and rises about 50 minutes later each day.
Hunt faint objects near new Moon; look at the Moon itself along the terminator.

questions.prompt: What causes the phases of the Moon?
choices: Earth's shadow covering part of the Moon
We see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth
The Moon giving off less light at certain times
questions.explanation: Half the Moon is always sunlit. The phase depends on how much of that half faces Earth. Earth's shadow is involved only in lunar eclipses.

questions.prompt: You see a half-lit Moon high in the sky at sunset. Which phase is it, and when will it set?
questions.explanation: A Moon a quarter of the way around the sky east of the Sun is at first quarter. It trails the Sun by about six hours.

questions.prompt: When does a full Moon rise?
questions.explanation: A full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it comes up as the Sun goes down and stays up all night.

questions.prompt: You want to see the Milky Way on a trip to a dark site. Which nights should you choose?
choices: Any night: the Moon makes no difference
questions.explanation: Moonlight brightens the whole sky. Near new Moon the Moon is absent or a thin crescent that sets early.

questions.prompt: The Moon rose at 8 pm tonight. About when will it rise tomorrow?
questions.explanation: The Moon moves about 13° east along its orbit each day, so Earth must turn about 50 minutes longer, on average, to bring it back above the horizon.

questions.prompt: Where on the Moon do craters stand out most sharply through binoculars?
choices: At the center of the full Moon
Along the terminator, the line between light and dark
At the bright edge facing the Sun
questions.explanation: Near the terminator the Sun is low in the lunar sky and features cast long shadows that reveal their relief.
